summary:
Terengganu is one of the 13 states of Malaysia and stands under the federal framework: sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, with a maximum of 20 years plus whipping. Sodomy has been criminalised in Malaysian law since 1871. These provisions are not limited to Malaysian citizens, so a foreign visitor in Terengganu is exposed to them on the same terms as a resident.

The state layer adds a second offence that reaches only Muslims. Every one of the 13 states, Terengganu included, maintains a Sharia enactment criminalising cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", punishable by up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Enforcement sits with state Islamic religious departments, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing, which leaves the charge open-ended. A non-Muslim visitor falls outside this layer, but the police powers exercised alongside it do not.

Official messaging in Terengganu is openly hostile. In May 2025 a state executive councillor confirmed that warning signboards against homosexual practices, erected by the Kuala Terengganu City Council at strategic locations including near youth-frequented areas around a state university, were installed deliberately, and said the state wants people to consider such acts "dirty, wrong, and to be avoided". He described instilling hatred of homosexual acts as the point of the campaign.

The documented enforcement pattern against gender nonconformity is raid-based rather than individual. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B, the largest operation of its kind since 2022; media were pre-tipped, detainees' faces and personal details were leaked, and 31 foreign nationals were held among more than 130 people at one point before their embassies intervened. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, yet release was delayed, and police raided a second sauna in Penang days later. Queues, venues and any place where gender presentation is conspicuous carry the acute exposure risk for a visitor.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor the practical position is that the Sharia cross-dressing offence does not apply, the Penal Code does, and enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon with tourists rarely targeted. The risk that materialises is public outing through an organised raid, and it is not backed by protective machinery: there is no anti-discrimination law, no same-sex marriage, and a transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in Malaysia in fewer than two months, in a case documented under the heading "The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself" alongside police mistreatment and impunity.
tangentialFactors:
Civil-society opposition to the Terengganu campaign is on the record. On 14 May 2025 thirteen organisations, including Justice for Sisters and a national trans-rights group, wrote to the Kuala Terengganu City Council demanding removal of the signboards, calling them discriminatory hate speech and a violation of international human rights law, and condemning the state executive councillor's defence of them as incitement to hatred against LGBTQ people. A transgender activist had made the same demand days earlier.

Litigation has narrowed the Sharia layer without loosening the federal one. The High Court denied a request to declare the cross-dressing prohibition unconstitutional, while the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024, both on federalism grounds, leaving Penal Code offences fully intact. A separate constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014 following the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Enforcement elsewhere in Malaysia sets the tone for what state religious departments do with these powers. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister announced that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked; in the Nur Sajat case, 122 religious officers were mobilised to pursue her for "insulting Islam" before she fled abroad and received UNHCR protection. Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, LGBT events and media content are censored, and Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects.

Terengganu also retains hudud-style penal provisions enacted in 2002 that are not in operation.
localsOnly:
Muslim residents of Terengganu are subject to the state's cross-dressing offence, enforced by the state Islamic religious department, with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, an RM5,000 fine and six strokes of caning. Because the enactments never define transgender dressing, an arrest under them rests on an officer's reading of a person's presentation rather than on a stated legal test.

Residents live with the signboard campaign as ordinary official communication. The Kuala Terengganu City Council placed the boards at strategic locations and the state executive councillor has publicly framed them as a deliberate "constant reminder" intended to shape how the public judges gender and sexual nonconformity, so the hostility a trans resident encounters is institutional rather than incidental.

Protection machinery for residents is thin. There is no anti-discrimination law and no same-sex marriage in Malaysia, documentation of killings of trans women records police mistreatment and impunity, and recourse has effectively meant fleeing abroad for UNHCR protection, as in the Nur Sajat case. Justice for Sisters and allied organisations supply bailors, legal aid and public challenge where state channels do not.
outOfScopeNotes:
The reason the 2002 hudud-style provisions in Terengganu remain inoperative is not established in the material available for this record, so their current legal standing should be treated as unresolved rather than settled.

Enforcement frequency inside Terengganu specifically is unresolved: the inventory documents raid-based arrests in Kuala Lumpur and Penang, not in Terengganu, and supplies no Terengganu arrest, charge or caning figures.

Whether Terengganu's Sharia enactment also bars women from posing as men is not sourced. Three states are known to carry that additional prohibition, but the sources do not name them.

Several visitor-relevant questions are not sourced at all for this state: legal gender marker and passport rules for entry, visa or arrival screening that could out a traveller, bathroom and facility rules, access to hormone therapy or trans-related care, and any state-level complaint mechanism for discrimination.
